source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: On Moses-style semantic illusions, GPT-3 davinci-003 gave the intuitive wrong answer most of the time. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly flagged the false premise.
numbers: 50 bespoke illusions. davinci-003: 72% fell for it, 18% correct. ChatGPT-3.5 74% correct, ChatGPT-4 88% correct. Atypical answers fell from 52% (babbage) to 10% (davinci-003). Humans (Prolific, 500 people, 4 tasks each): 64% intuitive vs 52% in the original study (n=61).
limits: Hand-scored. An intuitive answer counted only if the model also knew the true fact. Old OpenAI models; one run at temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Shallow acceptance of a false premise is a size and tuning effect, not fixed. Test our own base model with a premise-check probe before trusting it.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: A one-line instruction to check the question, and a few solved examples, repaired the illusion in davinci-003.
numbers: Suffix 'Think carefully and check the question for invalid assumptions': correct 18% to 54%, intuitive 72% to 28%. With 10 or more solved examples: correct 18% to over 64%.
quote: Think carefully and check the question for invalid assumptions
limits: One model (davinci-003), one illusion set. Tested only on a model that was weak at baseline.
agent_relevance: Supports a standing premise-audit step in S1 on every question. Check against G1 (doubt only on signal): a premise audit is a read step, not a doubt step.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: Strong models answered illusions correctly without writing out reasoning, so the fix lies in base skill and tuning, not in extra reasoning steps.
numbers: Authors report ChatGPT answers to illusions were mostly correct and did not contain chain-of-thought.
limits: Authors' interpretation; no reasoning ablation on strong models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more reasoning text is what catches a false premise.

source: Cai, Duan, Haslett, Wang & Pickering (2024) Do large language models resemble humans in language use?
finding: Preregistered Moses-type test (Hannon and Daneman 2001 items). ChatGPT rarely flagged the error, and flagged slightly more for a weak than a strong impostor (the human direction). Vicuna flagged almost nothing.
numbers: 54 trivia items, 3 conditions. ChatGPT error reports: baseline 0.00, strong impostor 0.13, weak impostor 0.17 (weak vs strong p=.036; not significant after removing exemplar items). Vicuna: 0.002, 0.022, 0.017 (no baseline difference).
limits: Instructions gave an example error to report. ChatGPT Jan 2023 version. The weak-vs-strong effect is fragile.
agent_relevance: Told to report errors, the 2023 model still glossed over about 83 to 87% of impostors. An explicit error-report instruction is not enough alone.

source: Cai, Duan, Haslett, Wang & Pickering (2024) Do large language models resemble humans in language use?
finding: Implausible-sentence reinterpretation (noisy channel). ChatGPT read implausible double-object sentences non-literally more than prepositional-object ones, as humans do. Vicuna did not.
numbers: Non-literal interpretation of implausible sentences: ChatGPT DO 0.92 vs PO 0.56 (p<.001); Vicuna 0.54 vs 0.47 (p=.178). Whole paper: ChatGPT human-like in 10 of 12 experiments, Vicuna in 7.
limits: Rates depend on item set; the interaction was fragile for Vicuna.
agent_relevance: Strong models repair likely slips toward the plausible meaning. Good for intent recovery, bad when odd wording was deliberate. Keep the literal text available for checks.

source: Zhang, Gibson & Davis (2024) Can Language Models Be Tricked by Language Illusions? Easier with Syntax, Harder with Semantics
finding: Tested comparative, depth-charge and NPI illusions with perplexity and surprisal. Models were more often tricked by the NPI illusion (structure) than by comparative and depth-charge illusions (meaning). No single model or metric matched humans.
numbers: Four LMs (including GPT-2, BERT, RoBERTa). NPI illusion effects appeared for the licensors 'did not', 'didn't' and 'never' in several models; no human-like illusion effect for comparative or depth-charge.
limits: Probability-based scoring, not generated answers. Small models. Authors say results do not settle whether LMs are cognitive models.
agent_relevance: Human good-enough errors are not copied by LMs in one stable way. Do not use a human illusion list as a proxy for model failure; measure the model.

source: Zhang, Gibson & Davis (2024) Can Language Models Be Tricked by Language Illusions? Easier with Syntax, Harder with Semantics
finding: The authors ask whether an LM should copy human errors or avoid them, and conclude the aim is recognising the intended meaning, not mimicking slips.
numbers: Qualitative discussion of four LMs with mixed matches to human data.
limits: Discussion section, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: The target for our agent is the intended meaning, not human-like slips.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher & Berant (2025) When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: Comprehension questions on garden-path sentences. Humans keep the wrong first parse (good-enough effect). LLMs show the same condition pattern. For humans, plausibility of the noun as object mattered more than syntax.
numbers: Humans (Prolific, 400 ms per word, 5 s question limit): 95.4% on simple questions, 37.0% on garden-path questions. Plausibility effect p=4.11e-16; GP vs non-GP p=.019 (implausible set) and 2.5e-13 (reflexive set). Best LLM o1-preview 78%, Gemma-27B 74%. Larger models agree more with human item difficulty (Kendall tau).
limits: 5 s answer limit and word-by-word display favour shallow parsing; not natural reading.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence the attach-the-plausible-reading-first habit exists in humans and models. Name the plausible-but-wrong parse as a failure to probe.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher & Berant (2025) When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: Garden-path sentences are harder for every tested LLM to paraphrase and to draw, mirroring the question-answer result. Size mostly raised item-level agreement with humans; pretraining tokens helped OLMo-7B but not OLMo-1B.
numbers: Paraphrase accuracy for GP sentences lower than non-GP for all models. Condition-level rank correlation high for all models.
limits: Two small extra tasks.
agent_relevance: A restate-the-task check catches shallow parses only when the model can parse correctly at all.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher & Berant (2025) Comparing human and language model sentence processing difficulties on complex structures
finding: Seven hard structures. Models struggle most on garden-path sentences, and thinking tokens help less on garden-path items than on other structures.
numbers: GPT-5: 93.7% on non-GP structures, 46.8% on GP. Highest human task accuracy 41.7%; LLM task means 28.3% to 65.3%. o3 74.5% without thinking, GPT-5 88.9% with thinking. Absolute thinking gain 0.17 on GP vs 0.35 on others. Weak models: thinking hurt. Rank correlation with humans up to 0.929 (o4-mini).
limits: OpenAI models cannot switch thinking off, so low vs high effort was used. GPT-5 is a strong exception on GP.
agent_relevance: More reasoning does not reliably fix a wrong first parse; for small models it can hurt. Gate extra reasoning on a real signal.

source: Li, Feng, Narang, Peng, Cai, Shah & Varma (2024) Incremental comprehension of garden-path sentences by large language models
finding: Four LMs (GPT-2, LLaMA-2, FlanT5, RoBERTa) on 24 garden-path sentences. Models showed lingering misinterpretation like people, and a comma (extra-syntactic cue) helped.
numbers: 24 sentences with optional-transitive and reflexive verbs; each has a misinterpretation and a correct-interpretation question. Abstract reports promising alignment with humans; attention analysis on disambiguating words.
limits: Small item set and small models. Exact scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: Punctuation and clause cues in the prompt reduce wrong first parses. Keep the user's punctuation.

source: Hu, Floyd, Jouravlev, Fedorenko & Gibson (2023) A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models
finding: Seven pragmatic tasks. The largest models (Flan-T5 XL, Tk-Instruct 11B, text-davinci-002) beat chance everywhere and neared humans on some. Wrong answers were literal readings, as for humans. Worst on humor, irony and maxims, where the speaker breaks an expectation.
numbers: Smallest models at chance; stark jump past 1B parameters. text-davinci-002 picked the human-preferred punchline only 55% of the time. No-context control: 30 humans. Removing the story hurt irony most, then deceits and maxims, for models and humans alike.
limits: Zero-shot, 2022 models, MTurk humans. The correct answer is a norm; individual variation is not modelled.
agent_relevance: Irony and maxim violations need the context kept in the prompt. Without context the model loses the same cases humans do.

source: Ruis, Khan, Biderman, Hooker, Rocktaschel & Grefenstette (2023) The Goldilocks of pragmatic understanding: fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Binary implicature task. Base, dialogue-tuned and benchmark-instruction-tuned models were near chance; only models tuned with an instruction per example did well. GPT-4 reached human level with chain-of-thought.
numbers: Humans 86.2% +/- 2.3 (best-minus-average rater gap 6%). Pre-trained models about 60% zero-shot. Example-level instruction-tuned models 72.3% to 81.8% zero-shot; 5-shot gains up to +15.2 points. Particularised (context-heavy) items harder than generalised ones for models and humans.
limits: Likelihood scoring of yes/no; 2023 models. A gap on particularised items remains for GPT-4 even with in-context examples.
agent_relevance: How a model was tuned mattered more than size. Context-dependent implicatures stay the hard case.

source: Ruis, Khan, Biderman, Hooker, Rocktaschel & Grefenstette (2023) The Goldilocks of pragmatic understanding: fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Chain-of-thought did not help the base-model groups and lowered one example-tuned model by 7.2 points. The authors also fault BIG-bench implicature for dropping ambiguous items and for weak human rating.
numbers: One example-IT model 74.5% (5-shot) to 67.3% (5-shot CoT), -7.2. Others +0.5 to +4.5. BIG-bench best-minus-average rater gap 18% vs their 6%.
limits: Benchmark critique by the authors; not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Report implicature results against a solid human ceiling. Do not assume CoT helps pragmatic reading.

source: SwordsmanImp (2024) Do Large Language Models Understand Conversational Implicature: a case study with a Chinese sitcom
finding: Chinese multi-turn dialogue implicature set tagged by violated Gricean maxim. GPT-4 matched humans; others trailed. Accuracy did not differ much by maxim.
numbers: 200 questions. Humans (10 native speakers, 32 questions each) 93.1%. GPT-4 94% (p=.802 vs humans). CausalLM-14B 78.5%. Baichuan2-13B 43%, InternLM-20B 62%.
limits: Small human sample; multiple choice; model explanations sometimes contradict their own choice.
agent_relevance: Maxim type is not the useful axis; model strength is. Do not build maxim-specific routing.

source: Askari, Zarriess, Alacam & Sieker (2025) Are BabyLMs deaf to Gricean maxims? A pragmatic evaluation of sample-efficient language models
finding: Child-style test of whether a model tells maxim-following from maxim-violating utterances. Models trained on under 100M tokens beat under-10M models but fell short of children and of a 3T-token LLM.
numbers: Five maxims adapted from Surian et al. (1996). More data helped some maxims.
limits: Small research models, not deployed assistants. Exact accuracies not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Quantity (how much to say) is a late-learned maxim; check answers for under- and over-informativeness.

source: Speckmann & Unkelbach (2021) Moses, money, and multiple-choice: the Moses illusion in a multiple-choice format with high incentives
finding: Four experiments (N=914) show the Moses illusion survives a multiple-choice format with the right answer on screen and survives money for accuracy. This rules out a cooperative-speaker explanation and low motivation as the main cause.
numbers: Moses answers: 52.3% across four questions; 52.6% in an online US sample. Participants knew the critical term in 73.2% of cases. Reder and Kusbit (1991) rates were lower (32 to 35%). About 12 euro bonus cut the illusion only about 16% and needed 300 people to show; 26.5% Moses answers in a high-knowledge subset; open-ended correct 69.7%.
limits: Fixed option order may allow position guessing. Incentives were modest. Student and online samples.
agent_relevance: Offering the right answer and paying for accuracy barely helps. A scaffold needs a structural premise check, not an exhortation to try harder.

source: Salient alternatives facilitate implicatures (2022)
finding: Showing the stronger alternative ('all') just before an underinformative 'some' sentence made people derive the implicature faster. Part of the usual implicature cost is low alternative salience.
numbers: Response time speed-up about 200 ms after the alternative vs a control (SD about 420 to 470 ms). Incorrect target responses 24% in one experiment, 14% in the other.
limits: Small effect; reviewers asked for more data; outliers cut at under 100 ms and over 10 s. Sentence-verification paradigm.
agent_relevance: Putting the unsaid stronger alternative in front of the model may make it easier to read 'some' as 'not all'. Cheap prompt device, untested for LLMs.

source: Comprehenders' error correction mechanisms are finely calibrated to language production statistics (2026, Cognitive Science)
finding: Readers repair subject-verb agreement slips toward the intended meaning, and repair rates track how often speakers make each kind of slip. Supports a noisy-channel account of inferring intent.
numbers: Trials not resolving the mismatch: 6.5% (Study I), 9.9% (Study II). Non-literal reading of the subject number about 22% (singular-singular-plural), 35 to 45% (singular-plural-plural), about 15% (plural-plural-singular).
limits: Agreement errors only; Bayesian fit to production error rates from earlier work.
agent_relevance: Intent recovery is rational: weigh prior plausibility against the chance of a slip. A good-enough reader is doing probability, not just being lazy.

source: Garden-path recovery and creative problem solving share a restructuring process (2026)
finding: People who recover well from garden-path sentences do better on creative (insight) problems, even after controlling for working memory and fluid intelligence, but not on analytic problems.
numbers: Garden-path skill explained 9% extra variance in creative problem solving beyond working memory and non-ambiguous comprehension, and 5% beyond fluid intelligence; simple shared variance about 11% and 5%.
limits: Mississippi State students; correlational; two experiments.
agent_relevance: Reanalysis of a wrong first reading and reframing a problem may share a process; a link to the reframing operators.

source: Frank & Goodman (2012) Predicting pragmatic reasoning in language games
finding: Rational Speech Act model: the listener infers meaning by reasoning about which word an informative speaker would choose. It predicts human bets very closely.
numbers: Speaker condition N=206, salience N=276, listener N=263 (745 on MTurk). Informativeness predictions vs speaker bets r=0.98 (P<0.001). Informativeness times salience prior vs listener bets r=0.99; r=0.87 after removing predictions of 0 and 100. Salience and listener judgements alone were uncorrelated (r=0.19).
limits: Simple reference game with few objects; high r partly from extreme points. Does not model depth limits or shallow processing.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable form of: what would a helpful speaker have said instead? Enumerate alternative utterances and check which the actual one rules out.

source: Hannon & Daneman (2001) Susceptibility to semantic illusions: an individual-differences perspective
finding: Individual differences in working memory and reading ability predicted how often people detect Moses-type errors. Closer (strong) impostors are missed more than distant ones.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded. Its 54 items and 3 conditions were reused by Cai et al. (2024).
limits: Known only through secondary use.
agent_relevance: Impostor similarity matters: near-synonym slips in a prompt are the ones to audit.

source: Erickson & Mattson (1981) From words to meaning: a semantic illusion
finding: Founding result. Most people answer 'two' to the Moses question even when warned some questions are faulty. Detection rose when the false word was less related to the right one.
numbers: Not opened. Exact rate not verified here; Snoopy cat vs dog vs mouse pattern confirmed secondhand in Cai et al. (2024).
limits: Number unverified; do not cite as exact.
agent_relevance: Reference point for human baselines.

source: Reder & Kusbit (1991) Locus of the Moses illusion: imperfect encoding, retrieval, or match?
finding: Argues the illusion comes from partial matching to memory, not poor encoding. Warning people to look for errors lowers the illusion but does not remove it.
numbers: Rates quoted by Speckmann and Unkelbach (2021): 33% (Exp 1), 35% (Exp 2 and 3), 32% (Exp 4) in the literal task.
limits: Seen only via the replication paper.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as the LLM instruction result (72% to 28%): a warning helps, never fully.

source: Christianson, Hollingworth, Halliwell & Ferreira (2001) Thematic roles assigned along the garden path linger
finding: Founding good-enough result. After 'While Anna dressed the baby spit up on the bed', many readers still say Anna dressed the baby. The first parse lingers after the correct one is built.
numbers: Not opened. Humans in Amouyal et al. (2025) show the same logic: 37.0% accuracy on GP questions.
limits: Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: After a revision, make the old reading explicitly dropped, not only add the new one.

source: Ferreira (2003) The misinterpretation of noncanonical sentences
finding: Implausible passives ('The dog was bitten by the man') are often read as the plausible reverse. People use a heuristic that noun-verb-noun means agent-action-patient.
numbers: Not opened; figures not recorded.
limits: Rates vary by plausibility and sentence type.
agent_relevance: Tell the model to read the role order, not the likely story. Add reversed-role items to test sets.

source: Karimi & Ferreira (2016) Good-enough linguistic representations and online cognitive equilibrium in language processing
finding: Review of why comprehenders keep shallow representations when the task allows, and how task demands change depth.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Known by title and abstract only.
agent_relevance: Reading depth depends on what the task asks. Pose the question so a shallow reading is not enough.

source: Degen & Tanenhaus (2015) Processing scalar implicature: a constraint-based approach
finding: Rival to default-implicature and relevance-theory accounts: 'some' becomes 'not all' more slowly when exact numbers are available as alternatives, which supports a constraint-based view.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: Known by title and abstract only.
agent_relevance: Alternatives available in context change which implicature is drawn.
